newsitem.title: USA: Simpson case producer did not break law, court says.
newsitem.headline: Simpson case producer did not break law, court says.

text.p: A television producer who secretly taped his conversation with a cabin attendant about a flight O.J. Simpson took after his wife was murdered did not violate eavesdropping laws, a U.S. appeals court ruled Tuesday.

Beverly Deteresa was an attendant on an American Airlines flight from Los Angeles to Chicago that Simpson took shortly after his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman were murdered on June 12, 1994.

Deteresa, of Irvine, Calif., sued American Broadcasting Cos. Inc. -- a unit of Walt Disney Co. -- and producer Anthony Radziwill after ABC broadcast a portion of a videotape it secretly recorded of Radziwill talking to Deteresa, who refused to be interviewed on television.

Radziwill also made a surreptitious audio recording of the June 1994 conversation, but no part of it was played on the air. ABC did however quote Deteresa as denying reports that Simpson kept his hand in a bag during the flight.
Deteresa's suit alleged unlawful eavesdropping, intrusion into private affairs, fraud and unfair business practices.
The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco affirmed the ruling of a U.S. District Court which threw out Deteresa's suit.

"No one in Deteresa's shoes could reasonably expect that a reporter would not divulge her account of where Simpson had sat on the flight and where he had or had not kept his hand," the court said in its written ruling on Deteresa's appeal.
The videotaping of the conversation had "an insubstantial impact on privacy interests," the court said.

Simpson was acquitted of the murders of his ex-wife and Goldman in 1995 after a sensational trial. Earlier this year, a civil court jury found the former football star liable for the deaths and ordered him to pay the families of the victims $33.5 million.
Radziwill came to Deteresa's home a week after the murders to talk to her about appearing on a television show. He did not tell her that their conversation was being recorded.
Deteresa told Radziwill she was not interested in appearing on the show. But she did reveal that she was "frustrated" to hear news reports about the flight that she knew were false.

The next day, Radziwill told Deteresa that he had audiotaped their conversation. He said he had also told a cameraperson to videotape them from a public street near Deteresa's home. ABC broadcast a five-second clip of the videotape on its "Day One" program while an announcer summarized her account of the flight.
Lawyers for Deteresa and Radziwill could not immediately be reached for comment.
